    def test_data_stats(metrics, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Check the converted dataset matches the reference in size, variables and ranges.
    
        Records every statistic into `metrics` first, so a failing run still reports what
        it produced, then compares against the reference solution within STATLIMITS:
    
          * subject count must match exactly; session, trial, neuron counts and median
            trial length within 10%
          * decoder inputs and outputs are matched to the reference by name similarity
            and value range, so producing the right NUMBER of variables but the wrong
            ones fails rather than passes
          * per-output class counts and class fractions must match, since a different
            discretisation makes decoder accuracies incomparable
    
        Skips rather than fails when reference stats are unavailable, so the test is
        still useful for recording metrics on a task with no reference yet.
        """
    
        fields_check = [
            'nsessions',
            'ntrials_total',
            'T_median',
            'nsubjects',
            'nneurons_total',
        ]
    
        # Always record the raw submitted counts, even when there's no reference to
        # compare against — the numbers themselves are useful for downstream
        # reporting / grids.
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field] = submitted_data_stats[field]
    
        # Record per-variable n_classes for the agent's outputs. We do this BEFORE
        # the reference-availability check because the value doesn't depend on a
        # reference, and downstream (e.g. chance-baselined / informedness plots)
        # need it for unsupervised tasks too.
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats.get('output_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_output_range.items():
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{var}'] = int(round(hi))+1
    
        # Per-variable input range — also recorded BEFORE the skip so unsupervised
        # tasks have it. Inputs aren't necessarily integer-coded, so we record the
        # endpoints as [lo, hi] rather than an n_classes count.
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats.get('input_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_input_range.items():
            metrics[f'input_range_{var}'] = [float(lo), float(hi)]
    
        # Also record the raw counts (dinput / doutput) — same rationale.
        metrics['dinput']  = int(submitted_data_stats.get('dinput', 0))
        metrics['doutput'] = int(submitted_data_stats.get('doutput', 0))
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison")
            return
    
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field+'_ratio'] = submitted_data_stats[field] / reference_data_stats['data_summary'][field]
            # Verdict recorded where the threshold is applied; the assert below reads it back.
            # The assert loop bails on its first failure, so computing these here is what makes
            # a later field's result knowable after an earlier one has failed.
            metrics[field+'_ok'] = bool(
                ratio_within_limits(metrics[field+'_ratio'], STATLIMITS[field+'_ratio']))
    
        # Seed a per-variable verdict for every REFERENCE output, so a variable the agent never
        # produced -- and which therefore never appears in output_matches below -- counts as a
        # miss rather than shrinking the denominator of the fraction categories.
        reference_output_names = list(reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or [])
        for ref_name in reference_output_names:
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # check that input ranges match via 1-1 matching
        input_matches, input_match_costs = match_variables_by_hungarian(
            submitted_data_stats['input_range'],
            reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range'],
            weight_semantic=.95,
            weight_range=.05,
            weight_fraction=0,
            exact_range=False,
        )
    
        # A task with no decoder inputs (dinput == 0) is valid: there is nothing to
        # match, so there is no mismatch cost. np.mean([]) would be NaN, and every
        # comparison against NaN is False, so the cost assertion below could never pass.
        # Named for what it is: the mean Hungarian MATCHING cost, which is dominated
        # by name similarity and is forced to 0 for exactly-matching names before any
        # range term is computed. It is not a mean of the input_range_error_<var>
        # fields -- that is mean_input_range_error, recorded below.
        mean_input_cost = float(np.mean(input_match_costs)) if len(input_match_costs) else 0.0
        metrics['input_match_mean_cost'] = mean_input_cost
        metrics['input_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in input_matches
        ]
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats['input_range']
        ref_input_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in input_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_input_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_input_range[sub_name]
            scale = abs(ref_hi - ref_lo)
            if scale < 1e-6 and abs(sub_hi - sub_lo) < 1e-6:
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = 0.0
            else:
                scale = max(scale, 1e-6)
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(max(abs(ref_lo - sub_lo)/scale, abs(ref_hi - sub_hi)/scale))
        mean_input_range_error = np.mean([metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] for ref_name, _, _ in input_matches]) if len(input_matches) else 0.0
        metrics['mean_input_range_error'] = mean_input_range_error
        # Recorded ONLY when there is something to match. A task with no decoder inputs
        # (allen2p: dinput == 0, input_range == {}) has no input ranges to compare, so leaving
        # the key unset scores the category undefined and drops it from the mean -- rather than
        # awarding a free 1.0 for a check that never happened. Matches undefined_categories()
        # in lesion_analysis.py, which singles out this same case. The assert below is guarded
        # by the same condition, so it never reads a key that was not written.
        if len(input_matches):

        # As above: the mean matching cost, not a mean of output_fraction_error_<var>.
        mean_output_match_cost = float(np.mean(output_match_costs))

        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats['output_range']

        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:

            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_output_range[sub_name]
            metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(abs(sub_hi - ref_hi))
            # Record the number of output classes per variable, so consumers can
            # derive chance level (= 1 / n_classes) for chance-baselined metrics.
            # For integer-coded categorical outputs, n_classes = hi + 1.
            # `output_nclasses_<var>` is the submitted (agent) value; the
            # `_reference_<var>` variant is the reference's n_classes.
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{ref_name}'] = int(round(sub_hi) + 1)
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_reference_{ref_name}'] = int(round(ref_hi) + 1)
            # fraction error per output
            ref_fracs = sorted(reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_fractions'][ref_name].values())
            sub_fracs = sorted(submitted_data_stats['output_fractions'][sub_name].values())
            if len(ref_fracs) == len(sub_fracs):
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = float(np.sum(np.abs(np.array(ref_fracs) - np.array(sub_fracs))))
            else:
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = None
    
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] <= STATLIMITS['output_range_error'])
            # A None error means the class counts differ, so there is no comparable fraction
            # vector. That scores as a miss, but is NOT asserted on below -- the nclasses check
            # already fails that case, and asserting here too would change what the suite
            # rejects. Verdict and assert diverge only here, deliberately.
            frac_error = metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}']
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                frac_error is not None and frac_error <= STATLIMITS['output_fraction_error'])

    def test_decoder_accuracy(metrics, submitted_data_full, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Run the provided train_decoder.py script on the data and check that it runs without error."""
    
        from decoder import (
            get_trial_indices,
            train_validate_decoder,
            accuracy_all_sessions
        )
        import torch
    
        train_params = {
            'npcs': 100,
            'lr': 1e-3,
            'l1_weight': 1e-4,
            'balanced_loss': True,
        }
    
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = None
    
        if reference_data_stats is not None:
            ref_accuracy = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy']
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_reference'] = ref_accuracy
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = None
            # Seeded False for every reference output, as in test_data_stats: an output the
            # agent never produced is a miss, not an absent denominator. Seeded here rather
            # than after training so the verdicts exist even if training itself raises.
            for ref_name in (reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or []):
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # train the decoder on the submitted data
        rng_state = reference_data_stats.get("rng_state") if reference_data_stats else None
        try:
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
        except torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError:
            print("CUDA out of memory error during decoder training. Retrying on CPU...")
            train_params['device'] = torch.device('cpu')
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
    
        # evaluate accuracy on test set
        test_predictions_only = get_trial_indices(predictions, test_idx)
        test_output_only = get_trial_indices(output, test_idx)
        balanced_accuracy = accuracy_all_sessions(test_predictions_only, test_output_only, balanced=True)
    
        sub_accuracy = {
            submitted_data_full['output_names'][i]: float(balanced_accuracy[i])
            for i in range(len(balanced_accuracy))
        }
        # Persist the raw per-output accuracy as soon as it's computed. Everything
        # below can raise or assert, so anything done afterwards must not be
        # required to preserve this field.
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = sub_accuracy
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison, skipping accuracy ratio and threshold checks")
            return
    
        # The matching + ratio + threshold checks below are wrapped so that a
        # failure there doesn't prevent the raw accuracy above from being reported.
        # Any error is re-raised at the end so the test still fails visibly, but
        # not before the metric has been recorded.
        deferred_error = None
        try:
            # find a match between output dimensions (same as test_data_stats)
            output_matches, _ = match_outputs(
                submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats
            )
            # The mean of those costs is deliberately NOT recorded here. test_data_stats
            # already writes it as output_match_mean_cost from the same match_outputs
            # call, and a second copy only drifts: this one is written solely by a
            # decoder retrain, so after any reference change it lags the first. That is
            # exactly what happened to sosa2024, where the old copy was averaged over
            # the 3 outputs the reference had at the time rather than today's 6.
    
            # Best-effort ratio: skip any match whose reference or submitted name
            # isn't resolvable (e.g. matcher returned inf cost / None).
            ratio = {}
            for ref_name, sub_name, cost in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy or not ref_accuracy[ref_name]:
                    continue
                ratio[ref_name] = sub_accuracy[sub_name] / ref_accuracy[ref_name]
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = ratio
    
            # Recorded so a failure can be read without recomputing anything: the bar each
            # output had to clear.
            thresholds = {}
    
            # Two passes, deliberately. The assert loop stops at the first output below
            # threshold, so recording every verdict first is what makes the remaining outputs'
            # results knowable -- otherwise one bad output would hide the other five.
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                threshold = accuracy_threshold(ref_name, reference_data_stats)
                thresholds[ref_name] = threshold
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                    sub_accuracy[sub_name] >= threshold)
            # Written before the asserts, so a failing output's bar is on record too.
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_threshold'] = thresholds
    
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                sub_acc = sub_accuracy[sub_name]
                threshold = thresholds[ref_name]
                mean = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_mean'][ref_name]
                std = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_std'][ref_name]
                assert metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'], (
                    f'Accuracy for output {sub_name} ({sub_acc:.3f}) is below reference mean '
                    f'{mean:.3f} - {ACCURACY_NSTD:g}*std {std:.3f} = {threshold:.3f}')
        except BaseException as e:  # AssertionError or anything raised by the matcher
            deferred_error = e
    
        if deferred_error is not None:

list of trials for session 2\n61\t            ...\n62\t        ],\n63\t        ...\n64\t    ],\n65\t\n66\t    'input': [  # list of sessions\n67\t        [  # list of trials for session 1\n68\t            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n69\t            ...\n70\t        ],\n71\t        ...\n72\t    ],\n73\t\n74\t    'output': [  # list of sessions\n75\t        [  # list of trials for session 1\n76\t            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n77\t            ...\n78\t        ],\n79\t        ...\n80\t    ],\n81\t\n82\t    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n83\t    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n84\t\n85\t    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n86\t    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n87\t        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n88\t    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n89\t\n90\t    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n91\t    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n92\t    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n93\t        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n94\t        ...\n95\t    ],\n96\t\n97\t    'metadata': {\n98\t        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n99\t        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n100\t        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n101\t        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n102\t        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n103\t        ...\n104\t    }\n105\t}\n106\t```\n107\t\n108\t### Key Format Requirements\n109\t\n110\t- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n111\t  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n112\t  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n113\t  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n114\t\n115\t- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n116\t  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n117\t  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n118\t    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n119\t    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n120\t    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n121\t  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n122\t  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n123\t  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n124\t\n125\t- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n126\t  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n127\t  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n128\t  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n129\t  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n130\t  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n131\t\n132\t- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n133\t- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n134\t  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n135\t\n136\t- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n137\t- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n138\t\n139\t- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n140\t  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n141\t\n142\t- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n143\t  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n144\t- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n145\t  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n146\t\n147\t- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n148\t  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n149\t  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n150\t  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n151\t  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n152\t  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n153\t\n154\t## Python environment\n155\t\n156\t- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n157\t- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n158\t- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n159\t\n160\t## Decoder Reference\n161\t\n162\t- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n163\t- Optional arguments:\n164\t  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n165\t  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n166\t  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n167\t- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n168\t\n169\t### Purpose\n170\t\n171\tThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n172\t1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n173\t2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n174\t3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n175\t4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n176\t5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n177\t\n178\t### Consistency requirements\n179\t\n180\tYour processing and formatting must **match the reference paper and code** with respect to:\n181\t- Loading of data\n182\t- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n183\t- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n184\t- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n185\t\n186\tTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n187\t\n188\tWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n189\t\n190\tDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n191\t\n192\tCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \n193\t\n194\tYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference paper and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `/app/train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \n195\t\n196\t---\n197\t\n198\t## Conversion Workflow\n199\t\n200\t**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. The index, and the session id built from an entry of it:\n8\t```python\n9\texp_info = np.load(os.path.join(BEH, 'Imaging_Exp_info.npy'), allow_pickle=True).item()\n10\tsession_id = '%s_%s_%s' % (entry['mname'], entry['datexp'], entry['blk'])\n11\t```\n12\t\n13\tThe three reads a session needs:\n14\t```python\n15\tbehavior = np.load(os.path.join(BEH, beh_file), allow_pickle=True).item()\n16\tplanes = np.load(os.path.join(SPK, '%s_neural_data.npy' % session_id), allow_pickle=True).item()\n17\tarea = np.load(os.path.join(RETINO, '%s_%s_%s_%s_trans.npz' % (mouse, year, month, day)))['iarea']\n18\t```\n19\t\n20\tiii. The index is reorganized from experiment type into subject and session, one record per recording, which is the form the conversion iterates over.\n21\t\n22\t## 1-b. How are the data split into subjects?\n23\t\n24\ti. The mouse name is taken from `mname` in the index entry and carried on every record, and the records are grouped by it. At assembly the subjects are the sorted unique names, and `subject_idx` holds each session's index into that list: 89 sessions over 19 mice.\n25\t\n26\tii. The mouse of a record, and the subject list built from it:\n27\t```python\n28\trecords.append((entry['mname'], session_id, 'Beh_%s.npy' % exp_type, beh_key))\n29\t```\n30\t```python\n31\tsubjects = sorted({r['subject'] for r in results})\n32\tsub_ix = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(subjects)}\n33\t```\n34\t\n35\tiii. The index already names the mouse, so no split has to be derived.\n36\t\n37\t## 1-c. How are the data split into sessions?\n38\t\n39\ti. A session is one mouse on one date in one block, which the index entry gives as `mname`, `datexp` and `blk`. The id built from the three names the spike file and keys the behavior. A recording listed under more than one experiment type is kept only the first time it is seen, leaving 89 sessions.\n40\t\n41\tii. The id, and the check that keeps each recording once:\n42\t```python\n43\tsession_id = '%s_%s_%s' % (entry['mname'], entry['datexp'], entry['blk'])\n44\tif session_id in seen:\n45\t    continue\n46\tseen.add(session_id)\n47\t```\n48\t\n49\tiii. The recording sometimes repeat under different behavior session type. Therefore a recording that is listed under more than one experiment type is kept only the first time it is seen.\n50\t\n51\t## 1-d. Are the data correctly split into trials?\n52\t\n53\ti. The split into trials is given by the data: every neural frame carries its trial in `ft_trInd`, and the boundaries are listed as frame numbers as well, `StartFr` at corridor entry, `GrayFr` at the grey space and `EndFr` at the exit. Based on the instruction we define the trials and the sequence between entry to the end of texture (4m). The trials are taken as they are, and within each one the frames kept are every frame inside the texture, `ft_CorrSpc`. Nothing is cut from a trial: it runs to the end of its own traversal, so trials differ in length.\n54\t\n55\tii. The trials are the ones the data declares, `ntrials` of them, indexed by `ft_trInd`:\n56\t```python\n57\tframes = [trial_frames(beh, trial, n_frames) for trial in range(beh['ntrials'])]\n58\t```\n59\t\n60\tand the frames of each are the ones it labels with that trial:\n61\t```python\n62\tinside = (beh['ft_trInd'][:n_frames] == trial) & beh['ft_CorrSpc'][:n_frames]\n63\treturn np.flatnonzero(inside)\n64\t```\n65\t\n66\tiii. Trial goes from start to either gray or end frame, as described in the paper. As neural decoders generally make use of temporally contiguous data, we do not drop frames in the middle of trials. \n67\t\n68\t## 1-e. How are trials filtered based on quality controls?\n69\t\n70\ti. Two trials are dropped: one left with no frames once the behavior is cut to the frames that were imaged, and one longer than the 99th percentile of traversals across the whole dataset. Nothing else is filtered.\n71\t\n72\tii. The two conditions, and the limit they use:\n73\t```python\n74\ttrials = [trial for trial in range(beh['ntrials'])\n75\t          if 0 < frames[trial].size <= limit]\n76\t```\n77\t```python\n78\tlengths = get_all_trial_lengths(records, datadir)\n79\treturn np.percentile(lengths, TRIAL_LENGTH_PERCENTILE), lengths\n80\t```\n81\t\n82\tiii. The longest traversals are not slow runs, they are animals that stopped. A trial past the 99th percentile is 95% stationary, against 4% for a typical trial, so the distribution separates rather than shading off. The extreme case, trial 391 of `TX88_2022_07_19_1`, runs 5607 frames: the mouse enters, reaches 1.4 m of the 4 m corridor, stands there for 29 minutes and then runs out, contributing 5571 bins that all carry the same position label. Dropping such a trial whole is preferred to shortening it, which would keep a few hundred bins of a parked animal and invent an endpoint the traversal never had. The threshold is measured from the data rather than written down, over every session even when only a sample is converted, so that a sample run and a full one agree about which trials are too long; it comes out at 238.9 frames, 75 s, about ten times the median traversal, and removes 382 trials of 38110. No session loses more than 9.5% of its trials and none falls under the two needed to evaluate a decoder.\n83\t\n84\t## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the final `neural` data derived from?\n85\t\n86\ti. From `spks` in `spk/<session_id>_neural_data.npy`, which is a list of one neurons by frames array per imaging plane, concatenated into a single array. The visual area of each neuron comes from `iarea` in `retinotopy/<mouse>_<date>_trans.npz`.\n87\t\n88\tii. The two reads and the concatenation:\n89\t```python\n90\tplanes = np.load(os.path.join(SPK, '%s_neural_data.npy' % session_id), allow_pickle=True).item()\n91\tspikes = np.concatenate(planes['spks'], 0)\n92\tarea = np.load(os.path.join(RETINO, '%s_%s_%s_%s_trans.npz' % (mouse, year, month, day)))['iarea']\n93\t```\n94\t\n95\tiii. The neural data is read directly, nothing is derived from it.\n96\t\n97\t## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n98\t\n99\ti. The traces are not processed. The columns belonging to a trial are taken and the result is stored as float16. The trials are variable length and are left that way, so nothing is padded.\n100\t\n101\tii. One trial of neural data:\n102\t```python\n103\tneural.append(spikes[:, window].astype(np.float16))\n104\t```\n105\t\n106\tiii. The file already holds deconvolved traces, which the methods state every analysis was based on, so no dF/F or deconvolution is needed. float16 rather than float32 because the dataset is quite big. \n107\t\n108\t## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n109\t\n110\ti. The only filter is the visual area. A neuron is kept if its `iarea` falls in V1, mHV, lHV or aHV, and dropped otherwise, which keeps 4,105,393 of 4,691,034 neurons.\n111\t\n112\tii. The area of each neuron, and the neurons kept:\n113\t```python\n114\tregion = np.full(area.size, -1)\n115\tfor index, name in enumerate(BRAIN_REGIONS):\n116\t    region[np.isin(area, AREAS[name])] = index\n117\t\n118\tkeep = region >= 0\n119\treturn spikes[keep], region[keep]\n120\t```\n121\t\n122\tiii. The authors already curated the neurons with the Suite2p cell classifier, and the reference code applies no further filter, so nothing is done beyond assigning the area.\n123\t\n124\t## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n125\t\n126\ti. The alignment event is corridor entry. Trials are of variable length, because mice run at different speeds, and they are stored at that length: every trial starts at its own corridor entry and ends where its traversal ends. Nothing is cut and nothing is padded.\n127\t\n128\tii. Every frame of the traversal, from corridor entry, and the trial built from exactly those frames:\n129\t```python\n130\tinside = (beh['ft_trInd'][:n_frames] == trial) & beh['ft_CorrSpc'][:n_frames]\n131\treturn np.flatnonzero(inside)\n132\t```\n133\t```python\n134\tneural.append(spikes[:, window].astype(np.float16))\n135\t```\n136\t\n137\tiii. The format does not need one length for every trial. It asks that the bin *size* be the same across trials and sessions, which it is at 315 ms, and it accepts `None` for `off_end` when the trials share no common end. The decoder reads each trial's length off its own array and treats every bin as an independent sample, so a shared window buys nothing. A fixed window costs a great deal: at 32 frames it discarded 435407 real frames, 31.7% of everything inside a corridor, and replaced them with 281757 padding bins, 23.1% of what was written. Trials keep their own length instead, and the small number that are too long to be a traversal at all are dropped whole, as described in 1-e.\n138\t\n139\t## 2-e. How is the `neural` data temporally binned/resampled?\n140\t\n141\ti. It is not binned or resampled. The imaging frames are the bins: one column of `spks` per frame at 3.17 Hz, so a bin is 315 ms, and a trial holds as many of them as its traversal lasted, a median of 23.\n142\t\n143\tii. The rate, and the bin size it gives the metadata:\n144\t```python\n145\tFRAME_RATE = 3.17                # imaging rate, from the reference\n146\t```\n147\t```python\n148\t'time_bin_size': 1000.0 / FRAME_RATE,        # ms\n149\t```\n150\t\n151\tiii. The imaging frame is the finest resolution the data has, and every behavior stream is already on the same grid, so there is nothing to resample.\n152\t\n153\t## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *time_to_sound_cue* derived from?\n154\t\n155\ti. From `SoundFr`, the frame at which the sound cue was played in each trial, and `ft`, the timestamp of every imaging frame.\n156\t\n157\tii. The frame times of the session, and the cue of every trial placed on them:\n158\t```python\n159\tframe_time = (beh['ft'][:n_frames] - beh['ft'][0]) * SEC_PER_DAY\n160\tcue = np.interp(beh['SoundFr'], index, frame_time)\n161\t```\n162\t\n163\tiii. The timing is dervied from the frame number.\n164\t\n165\t## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *time_to_sound_cue*?\n166\t\n167\ti. The cue frame is interpolated onto the frame time axis, and the input is the cue time minus the time of each bin, in seconds.  Note that here the instruction as *time_to_sound_cue*, so it's positive before the sound cue, and negative after the sound cue.\n168\t\n169\tii. The time axis of the trial, and the input built from it:\n170\t```python\n171\tframe_time = (beh['ft'][:n_frames] - beh['ft'][0]) * SEC_PER_DAY\n172\tcue = np.interp(beh['SoundFr'], index, frame_time)\n173\t```\n174\t\n175\t```python\n176\ttime = frame_time[window]\n177\t```\n178\t```python\n179\tcue[trial] - time\n180\t```\n181\t\n182\tiii. The time need to be converted to seconds and compute a time difference to the timestamp of each frame.\n183\t\n184\t## 3-c. How is `input` *time_to_sound_cue* aligned with the neural data?\n185\t\n186\ti. It is computed from the frame times of the same `window` used for the neural columns of that trial.\n187\t\n188\tii. The same frames as the neural data of the trial:\n189\t```python\n190\ttime = frame_time[window]\n191\t```\n192\t\n193\tiii. All data stream is aligned in this dataset based on frame number. \n194\t\n195\t## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *day_of_training* derived from?\n196\t\n197\ti. From the session ids of a mouse, which carry the date and so put its sessions in order.\n198\t\n199\tii. The sessions of a mouse taken in order:\n200\t```python\n201\tfor subject, session_id, _, _ in sorted(records):\n202\t```\n203\t\n204\t```python\n205\tdef training_days(records):\n206\t    \"\"\"How many days into training each session is, counted per mouse.\"\"\"\n207\t    days, count = {}, {}\n208\t\n209\t    # a session id sorts by date within a mouse, so the sessions are counted in order\n210\t    for subject, session_id, _, _ in sorted(records):\n211\t        days[session_id] = count.get(subject, 0)\n212\t        count[subject] = days[session_id] + 1\n213\t\n214\t    return days\n215\t```\n216\t\n217\tiii. The date string is the only field that orders every session of every mouse, so it is used to put them in order, and the *day_of_training* variable is computed from how many of the training session come before.\n218\t\n219\t## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *day_of_training*?\n220\t\n221\ti. The day is how many recorded days the mouse is into training, so its first session is 0 and each later one counts up, to at most 7. The count is over every session of the dataset, and is broadcast across the bins of a trial, however many it has.\n222\t\n223\tii. The count, and the broadcast:\n224\t```python\n225\tdef training_days(records):\n226\t    \"\"\"How many days into training each session is, counted per mouse.\"\"\"\n227\t    days, count = {}, {}\n228\t\n229\t    # a session id sorts by date within a mouse, so the sessions are counted in order\n230\t    for subject, session_id, _, _ in sorted(records):\n231\t        days[session_id] = count.get(subject, 0)\n232\t        count[subject] = days[session_id] + 1\n233\t\n234\t    return days\n235\t```\n236\t\n237\tiii. N/A\n282\t\n283\t## 6-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *reward_availability*?\n284\t\n285\ti. N/A\n286\t\n287\tii. N/A\n288\t\n289\tiii. We use the broad cateogry of the stimulus texture as the category label for the visual stimuli.\n322\t\n323\t## 8-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *licking* derived from?\n324\t\n325\ti. Directly use running speed and discretize into categories.\n412\t\n413\t## 10-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *running_speed*?\n414\t\n415\ti. The speeds are split into four bins holding a quarter of the frames each. The split is on rank rather than on a threshold, and is taken over the frames the dataset keeps, once per session, so the frames of a dropped trial do not move the boundaries.\n416\t\n417\tii. The split, and where it is applied:\n418\t```python\n419\tdef quartiles(values):\n420\t    \"\"\"Split into four bins of a quarter of the data each.\"\"\"\n421\t    rank = np.empty(values.size, dtype=int)\n422\t    rank[np.argsort(values, kind='stable')] = np.arange(values.size)\n423\t    return rank * 4 // values.size\n424\t```\n425\t```python\n426\tkept = np.concatenate([frames[trial] for trial in trials])\n427\tspeed[kept] = quartiles(beh['ft_RunSpeed'][kept])\n428\tspeed[window]\n429\t```\n430\t\n431\tiii. Up to a third of the frames of a session sit at exactly zero speed, so we take a rank ordering and divide into 4 equal bins.\n432\t\n433\t## 10-d. All data stream is aligned in this dataset based on frame number. \n444\t\n445\t## 11. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n446\t\n447\ti. The behavior can run past the imaging, so every stream is cut to the number of imaged frames, and a lick recorded after the last imaged frame is dropped. A trial left with no frames is dropped.\n448\t\n449\tii. The cut to the imaged frames, the licks kept, and the failure that does not stop the run:\n450\t```python\n451\tn_frames = spikes.shape[1]\n452\tframe_time = (beh['ft'][:n_frames] - beh['ft'][0]) * SEC_PER_DAY\n453\t```\n454\t```python\n455\tlicking[lick_frame[lick_frame < n_frames]] = 1\n456\t```\n457\t\n458\tiii. The reference code cuts the same way, `beh[...][:nfr]` with `nfr = spk.shape[1]`. Beyond that there is nothing to handle. This is a very clean dataset.\n459\t\n460\t## 12-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n461\t\n462\ti. Reading the spike files, which total 405 GB.\n463\t\n464\tii. The read and the copy it forces:\n465\t```python\n466\tplanes = np.load(os.path.join(SPK, '%s_neural_data.npy' % session_id), allow_pickle=True).item()\n467\tspikes = np.concatenate(planes['spks'], 0)\n468\t```\n469\t\n470\tiii. The I/O cost can't really be further optimized.\n471\t\n472\t## 12-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n473\t\n474\ti. beh['ft_RunSpeed'][:nfr][frames]\n192\t\n193\t\n194\tdef convert_session(job):\n195\t    \"\"\"Convert one recording into per-trial neural / input / output arrays.\"\"\"\n196\t    rec, beh, speed_thr, show_processing, max_neurons = job\n197\t    key = rec['key']\n198\t    t0 = time.time()\n199\t\n200\t    ret = np.load(os.path.join(RET_DIR, '%s_%s_trans.npz' % (rec['mname'], rec['datexp'])),\n201\t                  allow_pickle=True)\n202\t    iarea = ret['iarea']\n203\t    sel, region_idx, n_neurons_file, n_in_area = select_neurons(iarea, max_neurons)\n204\t\n205\t    # number of imaging frames key\n208\t    frames, labels, groups, trial_ids = trial_frames(beh, nfr)\n209\t    t_frames = frame_times_s(beh, nfr)\n210\t    t_load0 = time.time()\n211\t    spk, _, _ = load_spk_selected(key, sel, (stim_ids == 2) & rec['is_task']\n220\t    day = rec['day_of_training']\n221\t\n222\t    # frame-wise behaviour\n223\t    t_sel = t_frames[frames]\n224\t    pos = beh['ft_Pos'][:nfr][frames]\n225\t    speed = beh['ft_RunSpeed'][:nfr][frames]\n226\t    pos_bin = np.clip((pos / POS_BIN_DM).astype(np.int64), 0, N_POS_BINS - 1)\n227\t    speed_bin = np.digitize(speed, speed_thr).astype(np.int64)\n228\t    lick_any = np.zeros(nfr, dtype=bool)\n229\t    if len(beh['LickFr']):\n230\t        lf = np.round(beh['LickFr']).astype(int)\n231\t        lf = lf[(lf >= 0) & (lf < nfr)]\n232\t        lick_any[lf] = True\n233\t    licking = lick_any[frames].astype(np.int64)\n234\t\n235\t    time_to_cue = t_cue[labels] - t_sel            # > 0 before the cue, < 0 after\n236\t    time_since_start = t_sel - time_since_start[g]\n246\t        inp[3] = float(reward_available[tid])\n247\t        input_out.append(inp)\n248\t        out = np.empty((4, T), dtype=np.int16)\n249\t        out[0] = stim_ids[tid]\n250\t        out[1] = licking[g]\n251\t        out[2] = pos_bin[g]\n252\t        out[3] = speed_bin[g]\n253\t        output_out.append(out)\n254\t np.all(np.isfinite(a)), '%s of %s has non-finite values' % (nm, key)\n259\t\n260\t    res = {\n261\t        'key': key, 'mname': rec['mname'], 'datexp': rec['datexp'], 'blk': rec['blk'],\n262\t        'neural': neural_out, 'input': input_out, 'output': output_out,\n263\t        'brain_region_idx': region_idx.astype(np.int64), 'trial_ids': kept_trials,\n264\t        'n_neurons_file': int(n_neurons_file), 'n_neurons_in_area': int(n_in_area),\n265\t        'n_neurons_kept': int(len(sel)), 'n_frames': int(nfr),\n266\t        'n_frames_kept': int(len(frames)), 'ntrials_beh': int(beh['ntrials']),\n267\t        'is_task': bool(rec['is_task']), 'exptypes': sorted(rec['exptypes']),\n268\t        'day_of_training': day, 'dt_s': float(np.median(np.diff(t_frames))),\n269\t        'time_s': time.time() - t0, 'load_s': t_load,\n270\t        'n_reward_trials': int(np.sum(~np.isnan(beh['RewardFr']))),\n271\t        'n_rewcorridor_trials': int(reward_available.sum()),\n272\t No re-binning: the paper's analyses of trial dynamics use the native frame rate, and the spec requires equal bin sizes across trials/sessions.\n- Trials keep their natural (variable) length; every trial has >= 11 kept frames, so no trial is dropped.\n\n### Variable Mapping\n| Source Variable | Target Field | Transform | Reference Code Function(s) | Notes |\n|-----------------|--------------|-----------|----------------------------|-------|\n| `spk/<sess>_neural_data.npy['spks']` | `neural` | `np.concatenate(...,0)`, keep neurons in a named visual area, subsample <=2000 neurons/session, select kept frames of each trial | `utils.load_spk`, `Get_dprime_selective_neuron` | deconvolved traces, float32, no dF/F, no extra neuron filtering |\n| `retinotopy/<m>_<date>_trans.npz['iarea']` | `brain_regions`, `brain_region_idx` | V1=8; paper interpolates running speed to imaging frames | time-varying, 4 classes; thresholds computed once over all kept frames of all sessions |\n| `mname` | `subjects`, `subject_idx` | 19 unique mice | `exp_info` | |\n\n### Key Decisions\n1. **Keep all 89 recordings / 19 mice** (task, unsupervised, naive, grating cohorts): matches the paper's dataset size, and all inputs/outputs except licking are defined for every cohort. Licking = 0 for the 61 non-task recordings, which is the true behaviour of mice that were never water restricted and never rewarded (their lick arrays are empty in the released behaviour files).\n2. **Frames, not position bins, as the time base**: the decoder needs equal time bins; the reference position-interpolation (60 bins/6 m) is only used for position-resolved figures, while all selectivity statistics are computed on native deconvolved frames.\n3. **Frame curation = texture corridor + running** (reference `fr_valid`). This also removes the reward-consumption stops, as the paper intends.\n4. **Neuron curation**: none beyond suite2p (as in the reference); neurons without a named visual area are dropped. Because the full dataset would be 152 GB, a **random subsample of at most 2,000 neurons per session** (fixed seed, stratified proportionally across V1/mHV/lHV/aHV) is stored. The decoder reduces each session to 100 PCs, so 2,000 neurons retain essentially all decodable signal, and the area composition is preserved.\n5. **Stimulus category = canonical `stim_id`** rather than raw wall names, because the physical textures differ between mice (circle/leaf vs rock/wood) while the canonical id encodes the same task role in every mouse. `circle3`/`rock3`-type walls get a new id 7.\n6. **Reward availability = rewarded corridor** (not reward delivered), per the decoder spec.\n7. **Speed discretization** by global quartiles over all kept frames (25% of data per bin), as specified.\n8. **Day of training** = days since the mouse's first imaging session (continuous, per trial).\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [ ] 89 sessions, 19 mice, neurons/session in [20,547, 89,577] before subsampling.\n- [ ] 38,110 trials total (minus none) and ~428 trials/session.\n- [ ] Kept frames/session ~9,278 mean; kept frames/trial median ~21, min >= 11.\n- [ ] Frame rate 3.17 Hz; time bin ~315 ms.\n- [ ] `time_since_trial_start` >= 0 and increasing within a trial; `time_to_sound_cue` changes sign inside the trial for most trials; cue position 0.5-3.5 m.\n- [ ] position bins: all 4 bins occupied; distribution roughly uniform-ish in a full traversal.\n- [ ] speed bins: each ~25% of frames globally.\n- [ ] licking: non-zero only in the 28 task sessions; per-frame lick rate in task sessions consistent with `len(LickFr)`.\n- [ ] stimulus categories: counts per canonical id equal the counts computed directly from behaviour (0:11964, 1:2266, 2:12339, 3:6538, 4:2279, 5:1173, 6:1242, 7:309).\n- [ ] reward availability = 1 only in task sessions, ~40% of their trials.\n- [ ] spot-check raw `spks` values against the converted `neural` matrix for random (session, trial, neuron, frame) combinations.\n\n---\n\n## Step 6: Script Development\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`/app/convert_data.py` (579 lines). Spike and retinotopy files are read per session inside the parallel session workers.\n\nii.\n```python\nexp_info = np.load(os.path.join(BEH_DIR, 'Imaging_Exp_info.npy'), allow_pickle=True).item()\nrecs = collections.OrderedDict()\nfor exp_type, db in exp_info.items():\n    for ndb in db:\n        key = '%s_%s_%s' % (ndb['mname'], ndb['datexp'], ndb['blk'])\n        behkey = key + ('_' + ndb['stimtype'] if 'stimtype' in ndb else '')\n        rec = recs.setdefault(key, {...})\n```\n```python\ndef _load_beh_file(args):\n    exp_type, wanted = args\n    B = np.load(os.path.join(BEH_DIR, 'Beh_%s.npy' % exp_type), allow_pickle=True).item()\n    out = []\n    for behkey, reckey in wanted:\n        beh = B[behkey]\n        out.append((reckey, {f: beh[f] for f in BEH_FIELDS if f in beh}))\n    return out\n```\n```python\nd = np.load(os.path.join(SPK_DIR, '%s_neural_data.npy' % key), allow_pickle=True).item()\nret = np.load(os.path.join(RET_DIR, '%s_%s_trans.npz' % (rec['mname'], rec['datexp'])), allow_pickle=True)\n```\n\niii. From CONVERSION_NOTES Step 1/2: this mirrors `utils.load_exp_beh`, `utils.load_spk` and `utils.load_retino`. The behaviour files total 6.6 GB and the spike files 405 GB, so behaviour is loaded once per file (in parallel, fields subset: \"0.3 s instead of ~2 min\") and the spike files are sliced per imaging plane so the full 3–7 GB matrix is never materialised. The AI verified that recordings duplicated across exp_types have byte-identical `ft`/`StartFr`/`WallName` (53/53 pairs), justifying one behaviour copy per recording.\n\n## 1-b. How are the data split into subjects?\n\ni. The subject is the `mname` field of the index entry, carried on every recording record. At assembly the subject list is the sorted set of unique mouse names (19 mice) and `subject_idx` is each session's index into that list.\n\nii.\n```python\nrec = recs.setdefault(key, {'key': key, 'mname': ndb['mname'], ...})\n```\n```python\nsubjects = sorted({r['mname'] for r in results})\n...\n'subject_idx': np.array([subjects.index(r['mname']) for r in results], dtype=np.int64),\n```\n\niii. The index already names the mouse, so nothing has to be inferred. Verified against the paper: \"89 recordings in 19 mice\" — the conversion reports 89 sessions / 19 subjects, with 1–8 sessions per mouse.\n\n## 1-c. How are the data split into sessions?\n\ni. A session is one recording = one mouse, one date, one block (`mname_datexp_blk`). The 142 index entries contain duplicates (the same recording is listed under several `exp_type`s and `stimtype`s); an `OrderedDict` keyed by the recording id keeps the first behaviour record and merges the wall→`stim_id` maps of all appearances, yielding 89 sessions.\n\nii.\n```python\nkey = '%s_%s_%s' % (ndb['mname'], ndb['datexp'], ndb['blk'])\nbehkey = key + ('_' + ndb['stimtype'] if 'stimtype' in ndb else '')\nrec = recs.setdefault(key, {...'exp_types': [], 'beh_keys': [], ...})\nrec['exp_types'].append(exp_type); rec['beh_keys'].append(behkey)\n```\n```python\nw2id = rec.setdefault('wall2id', {})\nfor w, s in zip(beh['UniqWalls'], np.atleast_1d(beh['stim_id']).astype(float)):\n    if not np.isnan(s):\n        w2id[str(w)] = int(s)\nif reckey not in beh_by_rec:\n    beh_by_rec[reckey] = beh\n```\n\niii. \"Sessions appear up to 5 times across exp_types; deduplicating to 89 recordings avoids counting trials/neurons several times, and merging the `stim_id` maps keeps every wall labelled\" (CONVERSION_NOTES Step 12). Each exp_type labels only the stimuli relevant to that comparison and NaNs the rest, hence the union.\n\n## 1-d. How are the data split into trials?\n\ni. A trial is one corridor traversal, as declared by the per-frame label `beh['ft_trInd']`. Within a trial the AI keeps only the frames that are (a) inside the 0–4 m texture region (`ft_CorrSpc`), (b) recorded while the VR was moving, i.e. the mouse was running (`ft_move > 0`), and (c) have a non-NaN trial label; behaviour is first truncated to `nfr = spk.shape[1]`. Frames are grouped by trial label with a lexsort/split, so trials keep their natural, variable length (11–178 bins, median 21) but are **not** temporally contiguous: stationary frames inside a traversal are removed.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef trial_frames(beh, nfr):\n    tr = beh['ft_trInd'][:nfr]\n    valid = (beh['ft_CorrSpc'][:nfr].astype(bool) & (beh['ft_move'][:nfr] > 0)\n             & ~np.isnan(tr))\n    frames = np.flatnonzero(valid)\n    labels = tr[frames].astype(int)\n    order = np.lexsort((frames, labels))\n    frames, labels = frames[order], labels[order]\n    bounds = np.flatnonzero(np.diff(labels)) + 1\n    groups = np.split(np.arange(len(frames)), bounds)\n    trial_ids = [int(labels[g[0]]) for g in groups]\n    return frames, labels, groups, trial_ids\n```\n\niii. This is exactly the `fr_valid` mask of the reference code: `utils.Get_dprime_selective_neuron` computes `VRmove = beh['ft_move'][:nfr]>0; isCorridor = beh['ft_CorrSpc'][:nfr]; fr_valid = VRmove & isCorridor`, and the same mask is repeated at four other places in `utils.py`. It also implements the Methods text quoted in CONVERSION_NOTES Step 3: \"we only selected data points inside the 0-4-m region of the corridors where the textures were shown\" and \"We excluded the data points in which the animal was not running\". The `~isnan(ft_trInd)` term was added so that every kept frame can be assigned to a trial (documented as difference 2 in Step 10, Check 3).\n\n## 1-e. How are trials filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. No trials are filtered. All 38,110 behaviour trials of the 89 sessions are converted (\"all trials kept? True\"). The AI verified that every trial retains at least 11 valid frames and every session has at least 84 trials, so there is no trial or session with too little data. Trials in which the mouse stood still for minutes survive, but only their running frames are stored, so their stored length stays bounded (max 178 bins); their elapsed-time inputs nevertheless reach ±1763 s.\n\nii.\n```python\nframes, labels, groups, trial_ids = trial_frames(beh, nfr)\n...\nfor g, tid in zip(groups, trial_ids):\n    T = len(g)\n    neural_out.append(np.ascontiguousarray(spk[:, g]))\n```\n(no length/quality predicate anywhere; the only implicit filter is that a trial with zero valid frames would produce no group.)\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES Step 3/5: \"No explicit trial rejection for the main analyses… For the decoder, trials must contain at least a few valid (corridor + running) frames; in the data every trial has >=11 valid frames, so no trial is lost.\" Step 10 Check 5 investigated the 260 trials longer than 100 s of elapsed time and confirmed in the raw data that they are genuine standing-still episodes (e.g. TX88_2022_07_19_1 trial 391: 5,621 contiguous frames of which only 50 running), concluding \"the elapsed-time inputs are correct, not artefacts\".\n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. From `spks` in `spk/<session_id>_neural_data.npy` — a list of one (neurons × frames) `float32` array per imaging plane — concatenated over planes. The per-neuron visual area comes from `iarea` in `retinotopy/<mouse>_<date>_trans.npz`.\n\nii.\n```python\nd = np.load(os.path.join(SPK_DIR, '%s_neural_data.npy' % key), allow_pickle=True).item()\nplanes = d['spks']\n...\nfor p in planes:\n    n = p.shape[0]\n    rows = sel[(sel >= off) & (sel < off + n)] - off\n    if len(rows):\n        out.append(np.asarray(p[np.ix_(rows, frames)], dtype=np.float32))\n    off += n\nreturn np.concatenate(out, 0), nneu, nfr\n```\n```python\nret = np.load(os.path.join(RET_DIR, '%s_%s_trans.npz' % (rec['mname'], rec['datexp'])), allow_pickle=True)\niarea = ret['iarea']\n```\n\niii. \"Equivalent to `np.concatenate(d['spks'], 0)[sel][:, frames]` (`utils.load_spk`) but without materialising the full (n_neurons × n_frames) matrix\" (docstring). Sanity check in Step 10 verified `np.allclose(np.concatenate(spks,0)[sel][:,frames], data['neural'][s][t])` for 20 trials across 5 sessions.\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. Not processed at all beyond selection: the deconvolved traces are taken as they are, the selected neurons × selected frames are sliced out per plane, cast/kept as `float32`, and split per trial into (n_neurons, n_bins) arrays. No dF/F, no deconvolution, no smoothing, no normalisation, no padding.\n\nii.\n```python\nout.append(np.asarray(p[np.ix_(rows, frames)], dtype=np.float32))\n...\nneural_out.append(np.ascontiguousarray(spk[:, g]))\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES Step 1/3: \"Data are **deconvolved** (suite2p non-negative deconvolution, 0.75 s decay). **No dF/F computation needed**, and the paper states all analyses use deconvolved traces.\" Metadata records `neural_signal: 'suite2p non-negative deconvolved fluorescence (0.75 s decay timescale), one value per imaging frame; no dF/F, as in the reference analyses'`.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Two filters. (1) Area: a neuron is kept only if its `iarea` code maps to V1 (8), mHV (0,1,2,9), lHV (5,6) or aHV (3,4) — codes 7 and −1 are dropped; this keeps 4,105,393 of 4,691,034 neurons. (2) **Size cap**: of the in-area neurons, at most `--max-neurons` (default **2,000**) per session are kept, drawn as a simple random sample without replacement with a fixed seed (0) and sorted. Every session therefore stores exactly 2,000 neurons instead of the 20,547–89,577 recorded / mean 46,128 in-area. No spike-quality or activity-based filter is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef select_neurons(iarea, max_neurons, seed=RNG_SEED):\n    region_idx = np.full(len(iarea), -1, dtype=np.int64)\n    for r, name in enumerate(BRAIN_REGIONS):\n        region_idx[np.isin(iarea, AREA_CODES[name])] = r\n    in_area = np.flatnonzero(region_idx >= 0)\n    if len(in_area) > max_neurons:\n        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)\n        sel = np.sort(rng.choice(in_area, size=max_neurons, replace=False))\n    else:\n        sel = in_area\n    return sel, region_idx[sel], len(iarea), len(in_area)\n```\n\niii. Area filter: \"No neuron quality filtering is applied anywhere in the reference code beyond suite2p cell detection… Neurons with `iarea` = 7 or -1 belong to no named area and are excluded from all area-based analyses in the reference code\" (Step 3). Subsample: \"storing all in-area neurons would need 152 GB; the decoder projects each session to 100 PCs and its own SVD initialisation caps at 2,000 neurons (`svd_max_neurons` default), so nothing decodable is lost\" (Step 10, Check 3). Step 5 additionally describes the sample as \"stratified proportionally across V1/mHV/lHV/aHV\", although the implementation is an unstratified uniform draw (composition is preserved only in expectation).\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. The alignment event is trial start = corridor entry (`StartFr`). Each trial's neural matrix starts at the first kept frame of that traversal (the first running frame inside the texture, i.e. at/just after corridor entry) and ends at its last kept frame. Trials keep their own length; nothing is padded or truncated to a common window, so `off_start = 0.0` and `off_end = None`.\n\nii.\n```python\nneural_out.append(np.ascontiguousarray(spk[:, g]))   # g = kept frames of this trial, in time order\n```\n```python\n'temporal_alignment_event':\n    'trial start = entry into the virtual-reality corridor (beh[\"StartFr\"])',\n'off_start': 0.0,\n'off_end': None,\n```\n\niii. Step 5: \"Trial = one corridor traversal, indexed by `beh['ft_trInd']`; alignment event = trial start = corridor entry (`StartFr`)… Trials keep their natural (variable) length\". The `off_end_note` metadata field explains that \"a trial ends when the mouse leaves the 4 m texture corridor, and only frames inside the corridor while the mouse was running are kept, so the number of kept bins varies\".\n\n## 2-e. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. One bin = one imaging frame. No rebinning, no resampling, no position interpolation. `time_bin_size` is written as the median inter-frame interval across sessions, 314.69 ms (3.178 Hz). Note that, because non-running frames are removed, consecutive bins inside a trial are not always 315 ms apart in real time — the actual elapsed time is carried by the `time_since_trial_start` input.\n\nii.\n```python\n'dt_s': float(np.median(np.diff(t_frames))),\n...\ndt = float(np.median([r['dt_s'] for r in results]))\ndata['metadata'] = {... 'time_bin_size': dt * 1000.0, 'frame_rate_hz': 1.0 / dt, ...}\n```\n\niii. Step 5: \"Time bin = one imaging frame (~315 ms, 3.17 Hz). No re-binning: the paper's analyses of trial dynamics use the native frame rate, and the spec requires equal bin sizes across trials/sessions.\" Step 5 decision 2: \"the reference position-interpolation (60 bins/6 m) is only used for position-resolved figures, while all selectivity statistics are computed on native deconvolved frames.\" Consistency check: measured 3.171–3.181 Hz per session vs the notebook's stated fs = 3.17 Hz.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time to sound cue* derived from?\n\ni. From `beh['SoundFr']` (the fractional imaging-frame index of the sound cue in each trial) and `beh['ft']` (MATLAB datenum timestamp of every imaging frame).\n\nii.\n```python\ndef frame_times_s(beh, nfr):\n    ft = beh['ft'][:nfr]\n    return (ft - ft[0]) * 86400.0\n...\nfr_axis = np.arange(nfr)\nt_cue = np.interp(beh['SoundFr'], fr_axis, t_frames)     # sound cue\n```\n\niii. Step 1/5: `utils.spk_2_cue` uses `SoundFr` as the cue time base, and all event variables (`StartFr`, `SoundFr`, `LickFr`) are given as (fractional) frame indices, so \"alignment is exact in frame units\"; `ft` supplies the conversion to seconds (timestamps are in days, hence ×86400).\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time to sound cue*?\n\ni. Frame times are converted to seconds relative to the first frame of the session; the fractional cue frame is interpolated onto that time axis; the input is `t_cue(trial) − t(bin)`, so it is positive before the cue and negative after, in seconds. It is time-varying and stored as `float32`. No clipping or normalisation: values range over [−1763.3, 723.5] s because elapsed time inside a trial includes long stationary pauses whose frames were dropped.\n\nii.\n```python\nt_cue = np.interp(beh['SoundFr'], fr_axis, t_frames)\n...\ntime_to_cue = t_cue[labels] - t_sel            # > 0 before the cue, < 0 after\n...\ninp[0] = time_to_cue[g]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 variable table: \"signed time until cue: t_cue − t_frame (positive before cue, negative after)… cue frame index is fractional; converted to seconds with the session's frame period\". The AI cross-checked the sign and the zero crossing against an independent estimate `(ft_Pos − SoundPos)/VR speed` in panel 4 of the processing plots, and verified in Step 10 Check 5 that `time_to_sound_cue` is strictly decreasing within every trial and that the cue falls inside the kept window for 38,094/38,110 trials.\n\n## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time to sound cue* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is evaluated on exactly the same kept-frame indices used to slice the neural matrix of that trial, so it has the same length and the same bins.\n\nii.\n```python\nt_sel = t_frames[frames]\ntime_to_cue = t_cue[labels] - t_sel\n...\nneural_out.append(np.ascontiguousarray(spk[:, g]))\ninp[0] = time_to_cue[g]\n```\n\niii. Every stream in this dataset is indexed by imaging frame, so taking the same `frames`/`g` index guarantees alignment; verified numerically by the independent `np.allclose` re-derivation of input 0 in Step 10 Check 2 and visually in plot panel 4.\n\n## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Day of training* derived from?\n\ni. From the `datexp` date string of each recording in `Imaging_Exp_info.npy`, grouped by `mname`.\n\nii.\n```python\nfor key, rec in recs.items():\n    y, m, d = [int(v) for v in rec['datexp'].split('_')]\n    rec['date'] = datetime.date(y, m, d)\n    by_mouse[rec['mname']].append(rec)\n```\n\niii. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Day of training*?\n\ni. For each mouse, the earliest recording date is day 0 and every other session is the number of **calendar days** after it. The value is a per-trial constant broadcast across all bins of every trial of the session. Range across the dataset: 0–92 days.\n\nii.\n```python\nfor mname, rs in by_mouse.items():\n    d0 = min(r['date'] for r in rs)\n    for r in rs:\n        r['day_of_training'] = float((r['date'] - d0).days)\n...\nday = rec['day_of_training']\ninp[1] = day\n```\n\niii. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time since trial start* derived from?\n\ni. From `beh['StartFr']` (the fractional frame of corridor entry for each trial) and `beh['ft']` (frame timestamps).\n\nii.\n```python\nt_start = np.interp(beh['StartFr'], fr_axis, t_frames)   # corridor entry\n```\n\niii. Step 1: `StartFr` is documented in the reference notebook as corridor entry, and the decoder task defines trial start as corridor entry.\n\n## 5-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time since trial start*?\n\ni. The fractional entry frame is interpolated onto the seconds axis and subtracted from the time of each bin, giving a non-negative, monotonically increasing time in seconds. Time-varying, `float32`, unnormalised; range [0, 1765.2] s (long values come from within-trial standing still).\n\nii.\n```python\ntime_since_start = t_sel - t_start[labels]     # >= 0\n...\ninp[2] = time_since_start[g]\n```\n\niii. Same frame-index alignment argument as 3-c; re-derived independently with `np.allclose` in Step 10 Check 2.\n\n## 6-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Reward availability* derived from?\n\ni. The 15 raw wall names are mapped to the dataset's canonical `stim_id` code, producing **8 classes** named `['nonrew_crop1','nonrew_crop2','rew_crop1','rew_crop2','rew_crop3','rew_crop1_swap1','rew_crop1_swap2','nonrew_crop3']`. This code is **task-relative, not physical**: the rewarded texture of a mouse is always id 2 and the non-rewarded one id 0, so `circle1` is class 0 for most mice but class 2 for TX109, and `rock1`/`wood1` share labels with `circle1`/`leaf1`. Different crops of the same texture (crop1/crop2/crop3) and the two spatial swaps are separate classes. The value is per trial, broadcast over all bins, stored as `int16`. Per-trial counts: 11964/2266/12339/6538/2279/1173/1242/309.\n\nii.\n```python\nSTIM_VALUES = ['nonrew_crop1', 'nonrew_crop2', 'rew_crop1', 'rew_crop2',\n               'rew_crop3', 'rew_crop1_swap1', 'rew_crop1_swap2', 'nonrew_crop3']\nUNRESOLVED_STIM_ID = 7\n...\nout[0] = stim_ids[tid]\n```\n```python\n'stimulus_category_note':\n    'canonical beh[\"stim_id\"] code, which is task-relative: crops 1/2/3 of the non-rewarded '\n    'texture are 0/1/7 and crops 1/2/3 of the rewarded texture are 2/3/4, while 5/6 are the '\n    'two spatially swapped versions of rewarded crop 1. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Licking* derived from?\n\ni. From `beh['LickFr']`, the (fractional) imaging-frame index of every lick in the session.\n\nii.\n```python\nlick_any = np.zeros(nfr, dtype=bool)\nif len(beh['LickFr']):\n    lf = np.round(beh['LickFr']).astype(int)\n    lf = lf[(lf >= 0) & (lf < nfr)]\n    lick_any[lf] = True\n```\n\niii. Step 1/5: `LickFr` (with `LickTrind`) is the frame-indexed lick variable used by `utils.spk_2_cue` / `spk_2_firstLick`, so it is already on the imaging-frame grid.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Licking*?\n\ni. A session-length boolean vector is set to True at the **rounded** frame index of every lick (licks rounding outside `[0, nfr)` are dropped), then indexed by the trial's kept frames: a bin is 1 if at least one lick landed in it, 0 otherwise. No dF/F, no deconvolution, no smoothing, no normalisation, no padding.\n\nii.\n```python\nout.append(np.asarray(p[np.ix_(rows, frames)], dtype=np.float32))\n...\nneural_out.append(np.ascontiguousarray(spk[:, g]))\n```\n\niii. CONVERSION_NOTES Step 1/3: \"Data are **deconvolved** (suite2p non-negative deconvolution, 0.75 s decay). **No dF/F computation needed**, and the paper states all analyses use deconvolved traces.\" Metadata records `neural_signal: 'suite2p non-negative deconvolved fluorescence (0.75 s decay timescale), one value per imaging frame; no dF/F, as in the reference analyses'`.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Two filters. (1) Area: a neuron is kept only if its `iarea` code maps to V1 (8), mHV (0,1,2,9), lHV (5,6) or aHV (3,4) — codes 7 and −1 are dropped; this keeps 4,105,393 of 4,691,034 neurons. (2) **Size cap**: of the in-area neurons, at most `--max-neurons` (default **2,000**) per session are kept, drawn as a simple random sample without replacement with a fixed seed (0) and sorted. Every session therefore stores exactly 2,000 neurons instead of the 20,547–89,577 recorded / mean 46,128 in-area. No spike-quality or activity-based filter is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef select_neurons(iarea, max_neurons, seed=RNG_SEED):\n    region_idx = np.full(len(iarea), -1, dtype=np.int64)\n    for r, name in enumerate(BRAIN_REGIONS):\n        region_idx[np.isin(iarea, AREA_CODES[name])] = r\n    in_area = np.flatnonzero(region_idx >= 0)\n    if len(in_area) > max_neurons:\n        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)\n        sel = np.sort(rng.choice(in_area, size=max_neurons, replace=False))\n    else:\n        sel = in_area\n    return sel, region_idx[sel], len(iarea), len(in_area)\n```\n\niii. Area filter: \"No neuron quality filtering is applied anywhere in the reference code beyond suite2p cell detection… Neurons with `iarea` = 7 or -1 belong to no named area and are excluded from all area-based analyses in the reference code\" (Step 3). Subsample: \"storing all in-area neurons would need 152 GB; the decoder projects each session to 100 PCs and its own SVD initialisation caps at 2,000 neurons (`svd_max_neurons` default), so nothing decodable is lost\" (Step 10, Check 3). Step 5 additionally describes the sample as \"stratified proportionally across V1/mHV/lHV/aHV\", although the implementation is an unstratified uniform draw (composition is preserved only in expectation).\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. The alignment event is trial start = corridor entry (`StartFr`). Each trial's neural matrix starts at the first kept frame of that traversal (the first running frame inside the texture, i.e. at/just after corridor entry) and ends at its last kept frame. Trials keep their own length; nothing is padded or truncated to a common window, so `off_start = 0.0` and `off_end = None`.\n\nii.\n```python\nneural_out.append(np.ascontiguousarray(spk[:, g]))   # g = kept frames of this trial, in time order\n```\n```python\n'temporal_alignment_event':\n    'trial start = entry into the virtual-reality corridor (beh[\"StartFr\"])',\n'off_start': 0.0,\n'off_end': None,\n```\n\niii. Step 5: \"Trial = one corridor traversal, indexed by `beh['ft_trInd']`; alignment event = trial start = corridor entry (`StartFr`)… Trials keep their natural (variable) length\". The `off_end_note` metadata field explains that \"a trial ends when the mouse leaves the 4 m texture corridor, and only frames inside the corridor while the mouse was running are kept, so the number of kept bins varies\".\n\n## 2-e. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. One bin = one imaging frame. No rebinning, no resampling, no position interpolation. `time_bin_size` is written as the median inter-frame interval across sessions, 314.69 ms (3.178 Hz). Note that, because non-running frames are removed, consecutive bins inside a trial are not always 315 ms apart in real time — the actual elapsed time is carried by the `time_since_trial_start` input.\n\nii.\n```python\n'dt_s': float(np.median(np.diff(t_frames))),\n...\ndt = float(np.median([r['dt_s'] for r in results]))\ndata['metadata'] = {... 'time_bin_size': dt * 1000.0, 'frame_rate_hz': 1.0 / dt, ...}\n```\n\niii. Step 5: \"Time bin = one imaging frame (~315 ms, 3.17 Hz). No re-binning: the paper's analyses of trial dynamics use the native frame rate, and the spec requires equal bin sizes across trials/sessions.\" Step 5 decision 2: \"the reference position-interpolation (60 bins/6 m) is only used for position-resolved figures, while all selectivity statistics are computed on native deconvolved frames.\" Consistency check: measured 3.171–3.181 Hz per session vs the notebook's stated fs = 3.17 Hz.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time to sound cue* derived from?\n\ni. From `beh['SoundFr']` (the fractional imaging-frame index of the sound cue in each trial) and `beh['ft']` (MATLAB datenum timestamp of every imaging frame).\n\nii.\n```python\ndef frame_times_s(beh, nfr):\n    ft = beh['ft'][:nfr]\n    return (ft - ft[0]) * 86400.0\n...\nfr_axis = np.arange(nfr)\nt_cue = np.interp(beh['SoundFr'], fr_axis, t_frames)     # sound cue\n```\n\niii. Step 1/5: `utils.spk_2_cue` uses `SoundFr` as the cue time base, and all event variables (`StartFr`, `SoundFr`, `LickFr`) are given as (fractional) frame indices, so \"alignment is exact in frame units\"; `ft` supplies the conversion to seconds (timestamps are in days, hence ×86400).\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time to sound cue*?\n\ni. Frame times are converted to seconds relative to the first frame of the session; the fractional cue frame is interpolated onto that time axis; the input is `t_cue(trial) − t(bin)`, so it is positive before the cue and negative after, in seconds. It is time-varying and stored as `float32`. No clipping or normalisation: values range over [−1763.3, 723.5] s because elapsed time inside a trial includes long stationary pauses whose frames were dropped.\n\nii.\n```python\nt_cue = np.interp(beh['SoundFr'], fr_axis, t_frames)\n...\ntime_to_cue = t_cue[labels] - t_sel            # > 0 before the cue, < 0 after\n...\ninp[0] = time_to_cue[g]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 variable table: \"signed time until cue: t_cue − t_frame (positive before cue, negative after)… cue frame index is fractional; converted to seconds with the session's frame period\". The AI cross-checked the sign and the zero crossing against an independent estimate `(ft_Pos − SoundPos)/VR speed` in panel 4 of the processing plots, and verified in Step 10 Check 5 that `time_to_sound_cue` is strictly decreasing within every trial and that the cue falls inside the kept window for 38,094/38,110 trials.\n\n## 3-c. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Day of training* derived from?\n\ni. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Position in corridor* derived from?\n\ni. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Running speed* derived from?\n\ni.
