What processing is involved in computing `output` *Running speed*?\n\ni. Before converting any session, the speeds of the kept (corridor + running) frames of **all 89 sessions** are pooled and the 25/50/75th percentiles are taken as three global thresholds (12.42 / 25.35 / 40.85 cm/s). Each kept frame is then assigned a bin with `np.digitize` against those thresholds. This is a single global discretisation, so every bin holds exactly 25% of the dataset (0.250/0.250/0.250/0.250) although an individual session need not be uniform.\n\nii.\n```python\nspeeds = []\nfor key, rec in recs.items():\n    beh = beh_by_rec[key]\n    speeds.append(session_speed_values(beh, len(beh['ft']) - 2))\nspeeds = np.concatenate(speeds)\nspeed_thr = np.percentile(speeds, [25, 50, 75])\n...\nspeed_bin = np.digitize(speed, speed_thr).astype(np.int64)\nout[3] = speed_bin[g]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 7: \"Speed discretization by global quartiles over all kept frames (25% of data per bin), as specified\" — the decoder spec asks for \"4 bins, each corresponding to 25% of the data\". Using one global set of thresholds also makes the class label mean the same speed range in every session.\n\n## 10-c. How is `output` *Running speed* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Three fixed global thresholds [12.42, 25.35, 40.85] cm/s, applied with `np.digitize` (bin 0 = speed ≤ 12.42, …, bin 3 = speed > 40.85). The thresholds are recorded in the metadata. Because the kept frames are running frames only, the mass of exactly-zero speeds that would break a threshold-based split is largely absent, and the realised distribution is exactly 25% per bin.\n\nii.\n```python\nspeed_thr = np.percentile(speeds, [25, 50, 75])\nspeed_bin = np.digitize(speed, speed_thr).astype(np.int64)\n...\n'speed_bin_edges_cm_per_s': [float(x) for x in speed_thr],\n'output_values': [..., ['speed_q1', 'speed_q2', 'speed_q3', 'speed_q4']]\n```\n\niii. As above; the thresholds were also computed independently during exploration (Step 2: \"quartiles 12.4 / 25.3 / 40.8\") and the sample plot panel 2 overlays them on the raw speed trace coloured by bin.\n\n## 10-d. How is `output` *Running speed* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. `ft_RunSpeed` is one value per imaging frame and is sliced with the same kept-frame indices as the neural data, so it is bin-for-bin aligned.\n\nii.\n```python\nspeed = beh['ft_RunSpeed'][:nfr][frames]\nspeed_bin = np.digitize(speed, speed_thr).astype(np.int64)\nout[3] = speed_bin[g]     # same g as neural_out.append(spk[:, g])\n```\n\niii. Same frame-index argument; Step 10 Check 2 re-derived output 3 from the raw behaviour and the global thresholds with `np.array_equal`.\n\n## 11. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Several specific issues are handled: (a) behaviour arrays are 1–2 frames longer than the imaging, so every behaviour stream is truncated to `nfr` taken from the spike file; (b) frames with NaN `ft_trInd` cannot be assigned to a trial and are excluded by the frame mask; (c) licks rounding to a frame outside `[0, nfr)` are discarded, and sessions with empty `LickFr` produce all-zero licking; (d) wall names with no canonical `stim_id` in any exp_type (`circle3`, 309 trials) get their own category instead of being dropped; (e) recordings duplicated across exp_types are de-duplicated and their stimulus maps merged; (f) every produced array is asserted finite, and the neuron count in the retinotopy file is asserted to equal the neuron count in the spike file. Do NOT look outside this project directory.\n\n**Goal**: Understand how the original authors loaded and processed their data.\n\n**Actions**:\n- Look for documentation or README files in the `/app/code` directory\n- Read the provided reference code bases to see how the reference paper loaded and manipulated the data\n- Understand which functions are being called to read, curate, process, and manipulate the data\n- For neural imaging data, does delta F over F need to be computed? \n- For electrophysiology neural data, do cells need to be filtered based on quality? \n- Note to file important functions, their inputs, and outputs\n\n**Done when**: You have documented key functions and their purposes in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 1\".\n\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 2, update Step 1 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\n# Decisions\n\n## 1-a. How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?\n\ni. Everything is read from three directories under `data`: `beh` for the behavior, `spk` for the deconvolved calcium traces and `retinotopy` for the visual area of each neuron. `beh/Imaging_Exp_info.npy` is the master index and is read first, listing every recording grouped by experiment type. A recording is one mouse on one date in one block, and that triple is the session id, which also names the spike file. Each `Beh_<exp_type>.npy` holds the behavior of several sessions keyed by that id, so the conversion loops over behavior files and reads each one once; the spikes and the retinotopy are read per session.\n\nii. The index, and the session id built from an entry of it:\n```python\nexp_info = np.load(os.path.join(BEH, 'Imaging_Exp_info.npy'), allow_pickle=True).item()\nsession_id = '%s_%s_%s' % (entry['mname'], entry['datexp'], entry['blk'])\n```\n\nThe three reads a session needs:\n```python\nbehavior = np.load(os.path.join(BEH, beh_file), allow_pickle=True).item()\nplanes = np.load(os.path.join(SPK, '%s_neural_data.npy' % session_id), allow_pickle=True).item()\narea = np.load(os.path.join(RETINO, '%s_%s_%s_%s_trans.npz' % (mouse, year, month, day)))['iarea']\n```\n\niii. The index is reorganized from experiment type into subject and session, one record per recording, which is the form the conversion iterates over.\n\n## 1-b. How are the data split into subjects?\n\ni. The mouse name is taken from `mname` in the index entry and carried on every record, and the records are grouped by it. At assembly the subjects are the sorted unique names, and `subject_idx` holds each session's index into that list: 89 sessions over 19 mice.\n\nii. The mouse of a record, and the subject list built from it:\n```python\nrecords.append((entry['mname'], session_id, 'Beh_%s.npy' % exp_type, beh_key))\n```\n```python\nsubjects = sorted({r['subject'] for r in results})\nsub_ix = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(subjects)}\n```\n\niii. The index already names the mouse, so no split has to be derived.\n\n## 1-c. How are the data split into sessions?\n\ni. A session is one mouse on one date in one block, which the index entry gives as `mname`, `datexp` and `blk`. The id built from the three names the spike file and keys the behavior. A recording listed under more than one experiment type is kept only the first time it is seen, leaving 89 sessions.\n\nii. The id, and the check that keeps each recording once:\n```python\nsession_id = '%s_%s_%s' % (entry['mname'], entry['datexp'], entry['blk'])\nif session_id in seen:\n    continue\nseen.add(session_id)\n```\n\niii. The recording sometimes repeat under different behavior session type. Therefore a recording that is listed under more than one experiment type is kept only the first time it is seen.\n\n## 1-d. Are the data correctly split into trials?\n\ni. The split into trials is given by the data: every neural frame carries its trial in `ft_trInd`, and the boundaries are listed as frame numbers as well, `StartFr` at corridor entry, `GrayFr` at the grey space and `EndFr` at the exit. Based on the instruction we define the trials and the sequence between entry to the end of texture (4m). The trials are taken as they are, and within each one the frames kept are every frame inside the texture, `ft_CorrSpc`. Nothing is cut from a trial: it runs to the end of its own traversal, so trials differ in length.\n\nii. The trials are the ones the data declares, `ntrials` of them, indexed by `ft_trInd`:\n```python\nframes = [trial_frames(beh, trial, n_frames) for trial in range(beh['ntrials'])]\n```\n\nand the frames of each are the ones it labels with that trial:\n```python\ninside = (beh['ft_trInd'][:n_frames] == trial) & beh['ft_CorrSpc'][:n_frames]\nreturn np.flatnonzero(inside)\n```\n\niii. Trial goes from start to either gray or end frame, as described in the paper. As neural decoders generally make use of temporally contiguous data, we do not drop frames in the middle of trials. \n\n## 1-e. How are trials filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Two trials are dropped: one left with no frames once the behavior is cut to the frames that were imaged, and one longer than the 99th percentile of traversals across the whole dataset. Nothing else is filtered.\n\nii. The two conditions, and the limit they use:\n```python\ntrials = [trial for trial in range(beh['ntrials'])\n          if 0 < frames[trial].size <= limit]\n```\n```python\nlengths = get_all_trial_lengths(records, datadir)\nreturn np.percentile(lengths, TRIAL_LENGTH_PERCENTILE), lengths\n```\n\niii. The longest traversals are not slow runs, they are animals that stopped. A trial past the 99th percentile is 95% stationary, against 4% for a typical trial, so the distribution separates rather than shading off. The extreme case, trial 391 of `TX88_2022_07_19_1`, runs 5607 frames: the mouse enters, reaches 1.4 m of the 4 m corridor, stands there for 29 minutes and then runs out, contributing 5571 bins that all carry the same position label. Dropping such a trial whole is preferred to shortening it, which would keep a few hundred bins of a parked animal and invent an endpoint the traversal never had. The threshold is measured from the data rather than written down, over every session even when only a sample is converted, so that a sample run and a full one agree about which trials are too long; it comes out at 238.9 frames, 75 s, about ten times the median traversal, and removes 382 trials of 38110. No session loses more than 9.5% of its trials and none falls under the two needed to evaluate a decoder.\n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the final `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. From `spks` in `spk/<session_id>_neural_data.npy`, which is a list of one neurons by frames array per imaging plane, concatenated into a single array. The visual area of each neuron comes from `iarea` in `retinotopy/<mouse>_<date>_trans.npz`.\n\nii. The two reads and the concatenation:\n```python\nplanes = np.load(os.path.join(SPK, '%s_neural_data.npy' % session_id), allow_pickle=True).item()\nspikes = np.concatenate(planes['spks'], 0)\narea = np.load(os.path.join(RETINO, '%s_%s_%s_%s_trans.npz' % (mouse, year, month, day)))['iarea']\n```\n\niii. The neural data is read directly, nothing is derived from it.\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. The traces are not processed. The columns belonging to a trial are taken and the result is stored as float16. The trials are variable length and are left that way, so nothing is padded.\n\nii. One trial of neural data:\n```python\nneural.append(spikes[:, window].astype(np.float16))\n```\n\niii. The file already holds deconvolved traces, which the methods state every analysis was based on, so no dF/F or deconvolution is needed. float16 rather than float32 because the dataset is quite big. \n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. The only filter is the visual area. A neuron is kept if its `iarea` falls in V1, mHV, lHV or aHV, and dropped otherwise, which keeps 4,105,393 of 4,691,034 neurons.\n\nii. The area of each neuron, and the neurons kept:\n```python\nregion = np.full(area.size, -1)\nfor index, name in enumerate(BRAIN_REGIONS):\n    region[np.isin(area, AREAS[name])] = index\n\nkeep = region >= 0\nreturn spikes[keep], region[keep]\n```\n\niii. The authors already curated the neurons with the Suite2p cell classifier, and the reference code applies no further filter, so nothing is done beyond assigning the area.\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. The alignment event is corridor entry. Trials are of variable length, because mice run at different speeds, and they are stored at that length: every trial starts at its own corridor entry and ends where its traversal ends. Nothing is cut and nothing is padded.\n\nii. Every frame of the traversal, from corridor entry, and the trial built from exactly those frames:\n```python\ninside = (beh['ft_trInd'][:n_frames] == trial) & beh['ft_CorrSpc'][:n_frames]\nreturn np.flatnonzero(inside)\n```\n```python\nneural.append(spikes[:, window].astype(np.float16))\n```\n\niii. The format does not need one length for every trial. It asks that the bin *size* be the same across trials and sessions, which it is at 315 ms, and it accepts `None` for `off_end` when the trials share no common end. The decoder reads each trial's length off its own array and treats every bin as an independent sample, so a shared window buys nothing. A fixed window costs a great deal: at 32 frames it discarded 435407 real frames, 31.7% of everything inside a corridor, and replaced them with 281757 padding bins, 23.1% of what was written. Trials keep their own length instead, and the small number that are too long to be a traversal at all are dropped whole, as described in 1-e.\n\n## 2-e. How is the `neural` data temporally binned/resampled?\n\ni. It is not binned or resampled. The imaging frames are the bins: one column of `spks` per frame at 3.17 Hz, so a bin is 315 ms, and a trial holds as many of them as its traversal lasted, a median of 23.\n\nii. The rate, and the bin size it gives the metadata:\n```python\nFRAME_RATE = 3.17                # imaging rate, from the reference\n```\n```python\n'time_bin_size': 1000.0 / FRAME_RATE,        # ms\n```\n\niii. The imaging frame is the finest resolution the data has, and every behavior stream is already on the same grid, so there is nothing to resample.\n\n## 3-a. shuffles\nTEXTURE = {'circle1': 'circle', 'circle2': 'circle', 'circle3': 'circle',\n           'leaf1': 'leaf', 'leaf2': 'leaf', 'leaf3': 'leaf',\n           'leaf1_swap1': 'leaf', 'leaf1_swap2': 'leaf', 'rock', 'wood']\nLICKING = ['no lick', 'lick']\nPOSITION = ['0-1 m', '1-2 m', '2-3 m', '3-4 m']\nSPEED = ['lowest', 'low', 'high', 'highest']\n\n# the coarse visual areas of the reference, as the retinotopy codes them\nAREAS = {'V1': [8], 'mHV': [0, 1, 2, 9], 'lHV': [5, 6], 'aHV': [3, 4]}\nBRAIN_REGIONS = list(AREAS)\n\nINPUT_NAMES = ['time_to_sound_cue', 'day_of_training', ---\n\ndef list_sessions(datadir):\n    \"\"\"Every recording once, as (subject, session_id, beh_file, beh_key).\n\n    datadir: directory holding the beh/, spk/ and retinotopy/ subfolders.\n    \"\"\"\n    # the master index of every recording, grouped by experiment type\n    exp_info = np.load(os.path.join(datadir, 'beh', 'Imaging_Exp_info.npy'),\n                       allow_pickle=True).item()\n\n    records, seen = [], set()\n    for exp_type, db in exp_info.items():\n        for entry in db:\n            # a recording is one mouse on one date in one block, and names the spike file\n            session_id = '%s_%s_%s' % (entry['mname'], entry['datexp'], entry['blk'])\n\n            # the same recording is listed under several experiment types, so keep only the first\n            if session_id in seen:\n                continue\n            seen.add(session_id)\n\n            # the behavior file keys a swap session by its stimulus type as well\n            beh_key = session_id + ('_' + entry['stimtype'] if 'stimtype' in entry else '')\n            records.append((entry['mname'], session_id, 'Beh_%s.npy' % exp_type, beh_key))\n\n    return sorted(records)\n\n\ndef training_days(records):\n    \"\"\"How many days into training each session is, counted per mouse.\"\"\"\n    days, count = {}, {}\n\n    # a session id sorts by date within a mouse, so the sessions are counted in order\n    for subject, session_id, _, _ in sorted(records):\n        days[session_id] = count.get(subject, 0)\n        count[subject] = days[session_id] + 1\n\n    return days\n\n\n# --- trials ---\n\ndef trial_frames(beh, trial, n_frames):\n    \"\"\"Neural frames of one trial, from corridor entry to the grey space.\"\"\"\n    # the authors label every frame get_all_trial_lengths(records, datadir):\n    \"\"\"Compute the length of every trial in the dataset, in imaging frames.\n\n    Collect all trial lengths based on behavior data (approximately matches neural data)\n\n    records: list of (subject, session_id, beh_file, beh_key), every session of the dataset.\n    datadir: directory holding the beh/, spk/ and retinotopy/ subfolders.\n\n    Returns an int array of per trial frame counts, without the trials that were never imaged.\n    \"\"\"\n    # a behavior file holds several sessions, so it is read once for all of them\n    groups = {}\n    for record in records:\n        groups.setdefault(record[2], []).append(record)\n\n    lengths = []\n    for beh_file, group in groups.items():\n        behavior = np.load(os.path.join(datadir, 'beh', beh_file), allow_pickle=True).item()\n        for _, _, _, beh_key in group:\n            beh = behavior[beh_key]\n            n_frames = beh['ft_trInd'].size          # the behavior grid, so no spike bins of a quarter of the data each.\"\"\"\n    # a quarter or more of the frames can sit at exactly zero speed, and no threshold can\n    # cut a tie like that into equal parts, so the split is on rank rather than on value\n    rank = np.empty(values.size, dtype=int)\n    rank[np.argsort(values, kind='stable')] = np.arange(values.size)\n    return rank * 4 // values.size\n\n\n# --- neural ---\n\ndef load_spikes(session_id, datadir):\n    \"\"\"Deconvolved traces of the neurons of one session, and the visual area of each.\n\n    datadir: directory holding the beh/, spk/ and retinotopy/ spikes[keep], region[keep]\n\n\n# --- session ---\n\ndef process_session(subject, session_id, beh, day, datadir, max_trial_length):\n    \"\"\"One session as lists of per trial neural, input and frame_times_s(beh, nfr):\n    \"\"\"Imaging frame times in seconds, relative to the first frame of the session.\"\"\"\n    ft = beh['ft'][:nfr]\n    return (ft - ft[0]) * 86400.0\n\n\ndef select_neurons(iarea, max_neurons, seed=RNG_SEED):\n    \"\"\"Neurons assigned to a named visual area, with a random subsample.\"\"\"\n    region_idx = np.full(len(iarea), -1, dtype=np.int64)\n    for Behaviour events are given as (fractional) frame indices, so alignment is exact in frame units.\n- Frame curation: inside texture corridor (`ft_CorrSpc`, positions 0-40 dm) and running (`ft_move>0`).\n- Trials: corridor traversals; `StartFr` = corridor entry (= trial start = the decoder's alignment event), `GrayFr` = entry into grey space (corridor exit), `EndFr` = exit of the 6 m block.\n- Position interpolation (60 bins of 1 dm over the 6 m block) is used only for figures needing position-resolved activity; the d'/selectivity analyses use raw frames. For the decoder we keep the **native time base** (frames), as required by the task (time-varying variables in time bins).\n\n### Curation Steps\n\n**Neuron curation rules**:\n- Reference applies none beyond suite2p; the released `spks` are the accepted cells.\n- Area assignment via `iarea` (V1=8, mHV=0/1/2/9, lHV=5/6, aHV=3/4). Neurons with `iarea` = 7 or -1 belong to no named area and are excluded from all area-based analyses in the reference code.\n\n**Trial curation rules**:\n- No explicit trial rejection for the main analyses; analyses restrict to trials of particular stimuli. Figure-specific exclusions (first lick after 2 m, mice with too few leaf2 trials) are analysis-specific, not data curation.\n- For the decoder, trials must contain at least a few valid (corridor + running) frames; in the data every trial has >=11 valid frames, so no trial is lost.\n\n### Decoders Trained\n| Decoded variable | Accuracy |\n| (none reported in the paper) | n/a |\n\n---\n\n## Step 4: Check for Consistency\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nAll checks were run over **all 89 recordings** (script `cache/step4_checks.py`, `cache/step4b.py`).\n\n### Verified consistencies\n| Check | Result |\n|-------|--------|\n| Sessions / mice | 89 recordings, 19 mice -> matches paper exactly |\n| Neurons per session | min 20,547, max 89,577 -> matches paper exactly (\"20,547 to 89,577 neurons in each recording\") |\n| Neuron count in spk file == retinotopy file | identical for every session checked (10/10 spot-checked, all 89 verified later in Step 10) |\n| `ft_CorrSpc` == (`ft_Pos` < `Texture_Length`=40 dm) | True for 89/89 sessions -> the \"0-4 m texture region\" of the Methods |\n| `ft_move>0` == `ft_isMoving` | True for 89/89 -> \"running\" frame mask used by the reference |\n| median run speed on `ft_move>0` frames | 27 cm/s vs 0.0 cm/s on non-moving frames; This is exactly the `fr_valid = VRmove & isCorridor` mask of `utils.Get_dprime_selective_neuron` and the paper's \"only selected data points inside the 0-4-m region\" + \"excluded the data points in which the animal was not running\".\n- Time bin = one imaging frame (~315 ms, 3.17 Hz). No re-binning: the paper's analyses of trial dynamics use the native frame rate, and the spec requires equal bin sizes across trials/sessions.\n- Trials keep their natural (variable) length; every trial has >= 11 kept frames, so no trial is dropped.\n\n### Variable Mapping\n| Source Variable | Target Field | Transform | Reference Code Function(s) | Notes |\n|-----------------|--------------|-----------|----------------------------|-------|\n| `spk/<sess>_neural_data.npy['spks']` | `neural` | `np.concatenate(...,0)`, keep neurons in a named visual area, subsample <=2000 neurons/session, select kept frames of each trial | `utils.load_spk`, `Get_dprime_selective_neuron` | deconvolved traces, float32, no dF/F, no extra neuron filtering |\n| `retinotopy/<m>_<date>_trans.npz['iarea']` | `brain_regions`, `brain_region_idx` | V1=8; mHV=0,1,2,9; lHV=5,6; aHV=3,4 | `utils.neu_area_ID`, `load_retino` | neurons with iarea 7 or -1 are in no named area -> excluded (reference excludes them from every area analysis) |\n| `SoundFr`, `ft` | `input[0]` `time_to_sound_cue` (s) | signed time until cue: t_cue - t_frame (positive before cue, negative after) | `utils.spk_2_cue` uses `SoundFr` as the cue time base | cue frame index is fractional; converted to seconds with the session's frame period |\n| session date vs mouse's first session | `input[1]` `day_of_training` (days) | days between this recording's date and the first recording date of that mouse | `exp_info` `datexp`, `days` | continuous, constant within a trial |\n| `ft`, `StartFr` | `input[2]` `time_since_trial_start` (s) | t_frame - t_StartFr | - | continuous, time-varying; paper interpolates running speed to imaging frames | time-varying, 4 classes; thresholds computed once over all kept frames of all sessions |\n| `mname` | `subjects`, `subject_idx` | 19 unique mice | `exp_info` | |\n\n### Key Decisions\n1. **Keep all 89 recordings / 19 mice** (task, unsupervised, naive, grating cohorts): matches the paper's dataset size, and all inputs/outputs except licking are defined for every cohort. Licking = 0 for the 61 non-task recordings, which is the true behaviour of mice that were never water restricted and never rewarded (their lick arrays are empty in the released behaviour files).\n2. **Frames, not position bins, as the time base**: the decoder needs equal time bins; the reference position-interpolation (60 bins/6 m) is only used for position-resolved figures, while all selectivity statistics are computed on native deconvolved frames.\n3. **Frame curation = texture corridor + running** (reference `fr_valid`). This also removes the reward-consumption stops, as the paper intends.\n4. **Neuron curation**: none beyond suite2p (as in the reference); neurons without a named visual area are dropped. Because the full dataset would be 152 GB, a **random subsample of at most 2,000 neurons per session** (fixed seed, stratified proportionally across V1/mHV/lHV/aHV) is stored. The decoder reduces each session to 100 PCs, so 2,000 neurons retain essentially all decodable signal, and the area composition is preserved.\n5. **Stimulus category = canonical `stim_id`** rather than raw wall names, because the physical textures differ between mice (circle/leaf vs rock/wood) while the canonical id encodes the same task role in every mouse. `circle3`/`rock3`-type walls get a new id 7.\n6. **Reward availability = rewarded corridor** (not reward delivered), per the decoder spec.\n7. **Speed discretization** by global quartiles over all kept frames (25% of data per bin), as specified.\n8. **Day of training** = days since the mouse's first imaging session (continuous, per trial).\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [ ] 89 sessions, 19 mice, neurons/session in [20,547, 89,577] before subsampling.\n- [ ] 38,110 trials total (minus none) and ~428 trials/session.\n- [ ] Kept frames/session ~9,278 mean; kept frames/trial median ~21, min >= 11.\n- [ ] Frame rate 3.17 Hz; time bin ~315 ms.\n- [ ] `time_since_trial_start` >= 0 and increasing within a trial; `time_to_sound_cue` changes sign inside the trial for most trials; cue position 0.5-3.5 m.\n- [ ] position bins: all 4 bins occupied; distribution roughly uniform-ish in a full traversal.\n- [ ] speed bins: each ~25% of frames globally.\n- [ ] licking: non-zero only in the 28 task sessions; per-frame lick rate in task sessions consistent with `len(LickFr)`.\n- [ ] stimulus categories: counts per canonical id equal the counts computed directly from behaviour (0:11964, 1:2266, 2:12339, 3:6538, 4:2279, 5:1173, 6:1242, 7:309).\n- [ ] reward availability = 1 only in task sessions, ~40% of their trials.\n- [ ] spot-check raw `spks` values against the converted `neural` matrix for random (session, trial, neuron, frame) combinations.\n\n---\n\n## Step 6: Script Development\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`/app/convert_data.py` (579 lines).
